decks.title: Aldehydes and Ketones — Part 1: Structure, properties and preparation
goals: Name aldehydes and ketones by IUPAC rules and describe the carbonyl group
Explain the boiling points of carbonyl compounds compared with alcohols and alkanes
Write equations to prepare aldehydes and ketones from alcohols, alkenes, alkynes, acid chlorides, calcium salts, nitriles and esters

slides.heading: Carbonyl compounds
slides.body_md: Part 1 — aldehydes (R–CHO) and ketones (R–CO–R′): names, structure, properties and preparation.

visual.alt: Table of familiar carbonyl compounds

slides.narration: Namaste! The smell of vanilla, the solvent in nail-polish remover and the preservative formalin all contain the carbonyl group, a carbon doubly bonded to oxygen. In aldehydes this carbon carries at least one hydrogen; in ketones it is joined to two carbon groups. In this part we name these compounds, study the carbonyl group and learn many ways of making them.

slides.heading: Nomenclature
slides.body_md: **Aldehydes:** replace -e of the alkane by **-al**; the CHO carbon is C-1. **Ketones:** replace -e by **-one**, with the lowest locant for C=O. Common names come from the related acids (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde) or alkyl groups + ketone.

visual.alt: Table of names of aldehydes and ketones

slides.narration: An aldehyde is named by changing the ending of the alkane to al; the aldehyde carbon is always carbon one, so it needs no number. A ketone ends in one, with a number for the carbonyl carbon when needed, as in butan-two-one and pentan-three-one. Many common names come from the related acids: formaldehyde from formic acid, acetaldehyde from acetic acid.

slides.heading: Structure of the carbonyl group
slides.body_md: The carbonyl carbon is **sp²**: three σ bonds in a plane at about 120°, and a π bond to oxygen. C=O is **polar** (C δ+, O δ−) and is represented as a resonance hybrid of C=O and C⁺–O⁻. The carbon is attacked by **nucleophiles**; the oxygen by electrophiles (H⁺).

slides.narration: The carbonyl carbon is sp two hybridised, so the group is flat with angles of about one hundred and twenty degrees. Oxygen is more electronegative and pulls the pi electrons towards itself; we can think of the group as partly C plus, O minus. This makes the carbon a target for nucleophiles, and because the group is flat, attack can come from either face.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Methanal is a gas; lower members are liquids, higher ones solids. Carbonyl compounds are **polar** (dipole–dipole attractions) but **cannot hydrogen-bond with each other**: b.p. higher than alkanes and ethers of similar mass, lower than alcohols. Lower members **dissolve in water** (H-bonds from water to C=O); solubility falls with chain length.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points of compounds of similar mass

slides.narration: Compare compounds of similar molar mass. Butane boils lowest, with only weak dispersion forces. Propanal and propanone boil higher, because their polar carbonyl groups attract each other. Propan-one-ol boils highest of all, because its molecules hydrogen-bond. Small aldehydes and ketones dissolve in water, because water molecules hydrogen-bond to the carbonyl oxygen.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give IUPAC names: (a) $\ce{CH3CH(CH3)CH2CHO}$; (b) $\ce{CH3COCH(CH3)2}$; (c) $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)COCH3}$; (d) $\ce{OHCCH2CH2CHO}$.

**(a)** 3-Methylbutanal (CHO carbon is C-1).

**(b)** 3-Methylbutan-2-one.

**(c)** 3-Methylpentan-2-one.

**(d)** Butanedial.

nodes.label: Aldehyde: CHO = C-1; ketone: lowest locant

visual.alt: Flow for naming carbonyl compounds

slides.narration: Choose the longest chain containing the carbonyl carbon. For an aldehyde, number from the CHO carbon. For a ketone, number to give the carbonyl the lowest locant. So the first compound is three-methylbutanal, the second three-methylbutan-two-one and the third three-methylpentan-two-one. A chain with an aldehyde group at each end is a dial: butanedial.

slides.narration: Quick check. Remember that carbonyl compounds are polar but cannot hydrogen-bond with each other.

slides.heading: From alcohols, alkenes and alkynes
slides.body_md: **Alcohols:** 1° → aldehyde (PCC, or Cu at 573 K); 2° → ketone (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺ or Cu at 573 K). **Alkenes:** ozonolysis (O₃, then Zn/H₂O) splits C=C into two C=O groups. **Alkynes:** hydration with dilute H₂SO₄ + HgSO₄: ethyne → ethanal; other alkynes → ketones.

visual.alt: Table of preparations from alcohols, alkenes and alkynes

slides.narration: Gentle oxidation or dehydrogenation of alcohols gives aldehydes from primary alcohols and ketones from secondary alcohols. Ozone cuts a carbon–carbon double bond, and work-up with zinc and water gives two carbonyl compounds; this also helps locate the double bond. Water adds to alkynes with mercury two ions as catalyst: ethyne gives ethanal, and other alkynes give ketones.

slides.heading: From acid chlorides and calcium salts
slides.body_md: **Rosenmund:** RCOCl + H₂ over Pd/BaSO₄ (poisoned, so the aldehyde is not reduced further) → RCHO. **Dialkylcadmium:** 2RCOCl + R′₂Cd → 2RCOR′ + CdCl₂ (ketones). **Calcium salts:** dry distillation of a calcium carboxylate gives a ketone; with calcium methanoate, an aldehyde.

visual.alt: Table of preparations from acid chlorides and calcium salts

slides.narration: Acid chlorides are reduced to aldehydes by hydrogen over palladium deliberately poisoned with barium sulphate, so the reduction stops at the aldehyde: the Rosenmund reaction. Dialkylcadmium compounds turn acid chlorides into ketones. Heating calcium salts of carboxylic acids also gives ketones, such as propanone from calcium ethanoate; heating with calcium methanoate gives an aldehyde instead.

slides.heading: From nitriles and esters
slides.body_md: **Stephen reaction:** nitrile + SnCl₂/HCl → imine hydrochloride → (H₂O) aldehyde. **Grignard:** nitrile + RMgX → imine salt → (H₃O⁺) **ketone**. **DIBAL-H** (diisobutylaluminium hydride) reduces nitriles and esters to aldehydes at low temperature.

visual.alt: Table of preparations from nitriles and esters

slides.narration: Nitriles are versatile. In the Stephen reaction, tin two chloride and hydrochloric acid reduce a nitrile to an imine, which water hydrolyses to an aldehyde. A Grignard reagent adds to the nitrile carbon, and acid hydrolysis then gives a ketone, so ethanenitrile and ethylmagnesium bromide give butanone. DIBAL-H reduces nitriles and esters gently, stopping at the aldehyde.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing a preparation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Suggest a method: (a) propanoyl chloride → propanal; (b) ethanoyl chloride → pentan-2-one; (c) calcium propanoate → a ketone (name it); (d) propanenitrile → pentan-3-one.

**(a)** H₂, Pd/BaSO₄ (Rosenmund).

**(b)** Dipropylcadmium: $\ce{2CH3COCl + (CH3CH2CH2)2Cd -> 2CH3COCH2CH2CH3 + CdCl2}$.

**(c)** Heat: pentan-3-one, $\ce{(CH3CH2COO)2Ca -> CH3CH2COCH2CH3 + CaCO3}$.

**(d)** $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr}$, then $\ce{H3O+}$.

visual.alt: Table of conversions

slides.narration: Choose by the target. To stop an acid chloride at the aldehyde, use the Rosenmund reduction. To turn ethanoyl chloride into pentan-two-one, add a propyl group with dipropylcadmium. Heating calcium propanoate gives pentan-three-one, a symmetrical ketone. And propanenitrile with ethylmagnesium bromide, after hydrolysis, also gives pentan-three-one.

slides.heading: Quick check: preparation
slides.body_md: Pick the method that gives a particular aldehyde or ketone.
slides.narration: Quick check. Rosenmund and Stephen give aldehydes; cadmium reagents and Grignard reagents with nitriles give ketones.

slides.heading: Preparation summary
slides.body_md: Every route at a glance.

visual.alt: Flow summarising routes to aldehydes and ketones

slides.narration: Here is the whole picture. Aldehydes come from primary alcohols, acid chlorides by the Rosenmund reaction, nitriles by the Stephen reaction or DIBAL-H, and esters by DIBAL-H. Ketones come from secondary alcohols, acid chlorides with dialkylcadmium, nitriles with Grignard reagents, and calcium salts on heating. Alkenes and alkynes can give either, depending on their structure.

slides.heading: Quick check: from alkenes and alkynes
slides.body_md: Predict the carbonyl compound formed by ozonolysis or by hydration of an alkyne.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ozonolysis splits the double bond; only ethyne gives an aldehyde on hydration.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: C=O sp², planar, polar; carbon electrophilic.
B.p.: alkanes, ethers < aldehydes, ketones < alcohols; lower members water-soluble.
Aldehydes from 1° alcohols, Rosenmund, Stephen, DIBAL-H, ethyne hydration, calcium salts + formate.
Ketones from 2° alcohols, R′₂Cd + RCOCl, RCN + R′MgX, (RCOO)₂Ca, alkyne hydration; ozonolysis gives either.

visual.alt: Summary table of named preparations

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Aldehydes and ketones are named with the endings al and one. The flat, polar carbonyl group gives them boiling points between those of alkanes and alcohols. They can be made from alcohols, alkenes, alkynes, acid chlorides, calcium salts, nitriles and esters, and the choice of method decides whether an aldehyde or a ketone is obtained.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Explain why Pd is poisoned with BaSO₄ in the Rosenmund reaction.
For calcium salts, remember calcium methanoate gives aldehydes.
For Grignard + nitrile, include the hydrolysis step.
Compare b.p. using dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonding.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Explain the purpose of the barium sulphate poison in the Rosenmund reaction. Remember that calcium methanoate is needed to make aldehydes from calcium salts. Include the hydrolysis step in Grignard and Stephen reactions. And remember that carbonyl compounds cannot hydrogen-bond with each other.

goals: Draw the mechanism of nucleophilic addition of HCN and explain why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones
Write additions of NaHSO₃, Grignard reagents and ammonia derivatives
Write oxidation, iodoform and reduction reactions (Clemmensen, Wolff–Kishner, red P/HI)
Draw the aldol mechanism; predict aldol, cross aldol or Cannizzaro; use tests to distinguish carbonyl compounds

slides.heading: Reactions of carbonyl compounds
slides.body_md: Part 2 — addition to C=O, oxidation and reduction, reactions of α-hydrogens, and tests.

visual.alt: Flow of the reactions in Part 2

slides.narration: The polar carbonyl group gives aldehydes and ketones a rich chemistry. Nucleophiles add to the carbonyl carbon. Aldehydes are easily oxidised, while both aldehydes and ketones can be reduced. Hydrogens on the neighbouring carbon are acidic, leading to aldol reactions. And these properties give simple tests to tell the compounds apart.

slides.heading: Nucleophilic addition and reactivity
slides.body_md: A nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon; carbon becomes **sp³** in a tetrahedral alkoxide, which is protonated. **Reactivity: HCHO > RCHO > R₂CO**: alkyl groups (+I) reduce the δ+ on carbon and **sterically hinder** attack.

visual.alt: Two-step nucleophilic addition: the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon to give a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which takes a proton to give the product

slides.narration: The nucleophile attacks the partly positive carbonyl carbon, the pi electrons move onto oxygen, and a tetrahedral intermediate forms, which then picks up a proton. Methanal reacts fastest, then other aldehydes, then ketones. Alkyl groups push electrons towards the carbonyl carbon, making it less positive, and they crowd the approach of the nucleophile.

slides.heading: Mechanism: addition of HCN
slides.body_md: A trace of base generates CN⁻: $\ce{HCN + OH- -> CN- + H2O}$. (1) CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon (slow), giving a tetrahedral alkoxide. (2) The alkoxide takes H⁺ from HCN (fast), regenerating CN⁻. Product: a **cyanohydrin**, which can be hydrolysed to an α-hydroxy acid.

visual.alt: Flow of the HCN addition mechanism

slides.narration: Hydrogen cyanide itself is a poor nucleophile, so a little base is added to make cyanide ions. In the slow step, cyanide attacks the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion. This ion then takes a proton from hydrogen cyanide, forming the cyanohydrin and regenerating cyanide. Propanone gives propanone cyanohydrin, an industrial intermediate for Perspex.

slides.heading: Other additions: NaHSO₃, Grignard and ammonia derivatives
slides.body_md: **NaHSO₃:** crystalline bisulphite adducts (aldehydes and methyl ketones); decomposed by acid or alkali — used to purify. **Grignard:** HCHO → 1°, RCHO → 2°, R₂CO → 3° alcohols. **Ammonia derivatives** (Z–NH₂) add and then lose water (addition–elimination) to give C=N–Z.

visual.alt: Table of ammonia derivatives and products

slides.narration: Sodium hydrogensulphite adds to aldehydes and methyl ketones to form crystalline solids, which can be filtered off and broken down again with acid or alkali: a good way to purify them. Grignard reagents give alcohols. Ammonia derivatives such as hydroxylamine, hydrazine, phenylhydrazine and semicarbazide add to the carbonyl group and then lose water, giving solid derivatives with sharp melting points used to identify the original compound.

slides.heading: Worked example: addition products
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the product of butanone with (a) HCN, (b) NaHSO₃, (c) phenylhydrazine, (d) semicarbazide, (e) CH₃MgI then H₃O⁺.

**(a)** $\ce{CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CN}$, butanone cyanohydrin.

**(b)** $\ce{CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)SO3Na}$.

**(c)** $\ce{CH3CH2C(CH3)=NNHC6H5}$, butanone phenylhydrazone.

**(d)** $\ce{CH3CH2C(CH3)=NNHCONH2}$, butanone semicarbazone.

**(e)** 2-Methylbutan-2-ol.

visual.alt: Table of addition products of butanone

slides.narration: Each reagent adds to the same carbonyl carbon. Hydrogen cyanide and sodium hydrogensulphite simply add across the carbon–oxygen double bond. Phenylhydrazine and semicarbazide add and then lose water, giving a carbon–nitrogen double bond. A Grignard reagent adds a methyl group, and hydrolysis gives a tertiary alcohol, two-methylbutan-two-ol.

slides.heading: Quick check: nucleophilic addition
slides.body_md: Predict an addition product or compare reactivity towards nucleophiles.
slides.narration: Quick check. Methanal is most reactive; ammonia derivatives give compounds with a carbon–nitrogen double bond after losing water.

slides.heading: Oxidation and the iodoform reaction
slides.body_md: Aldehydes are oxidised easily to acids (even by Tollens’ and Fehling’s reagents); ketones resist mild oxidants and are cleaved only by strong oxidants on heating. **Iodoform reaction:** compounds with **CH₃CO–** (or CH₃CH(OH)–) react with I₂/NaOH to give yellow **CHI₃** and the carboxylate with one carbon fewer.

visual.alt: Table of iodoform test results

slides.narration: Aldehydes have a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so they are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids. Ketones resist mild oxidants. Any compound with a methyl group next to the carbonyl, a methyl ketone or ethanal, gives the iodoform reaction: the methyl group becomes yellow iodoform and the rest becomes a carboxylate. So butanone gives iodoform but pentan-three-one does not.

slides.heading: Reduction
slides.body_md: **To alcohols:** NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ or H₂/Ni: aldehydes → 1°, ketones → 2°. **To alkanes (C=O → CH₂):** **Clemmensen** (Zn–Hg, conc. HCl); **Wolff–Kishner** (NH₂NH₂, then KOH in ethylene glycol, about 453–473 K); **red P + HI** (heat).

visual.alt: Table of reduction products of butanone

slides.narration: Hydride reagents and catalytic hydrogen reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols. To remove the oxygen completely, three methods are used: the Clemmensen reduction with zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid, suitable for compounds stable to acid; the Wolff–Kishner reduction, which forms the hydrazone and then heats it with alkali, suitable for compounds stable to base; and red phosphorus with hydrogen iodide.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidation and reduction
slides.body_md: Predict a reduction product or an iodoform result.
slides.narration: Quick check. Clemmensen and Wolff–Kishner give alkanes; iodoform needs a methyl group next to the carbonyl.

slides.heading: Acidity of α-hydrogens; aldol mechanism
slides.body_md: α-Hydrogens are acidic because the **enolate** formed is resonance-stabilised (charge shared with O). **Aldol** (dilute NaOH): (1) OH⁻ removes an α-H → enolate; (2) enolate attacks the C=O of a second molecule; (3) the alkoxide takes H⁺ from water → **β-hydroxy carbonyl** (aldol); on heating, loss of water → **α,β-unsaturated** carbonyl.

visual.alt: Flow of the aldol mechanism

slides.narration: A hydrogen on the carbon next to the carbonyl group can be removed by a base, because the resulting enolate ion spreads its negative charge onto oxygen. In the aldol reaction, hydroxide removes such a hydrogen from ethanal; the enolate attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule; and protonation gives three-hydroxybutanal, the aldol. Heating removes water to give but-two-enal.

slides.heading: Cross aldol and Cannizzaro reactions
slides.body_md: **Cross aldol:** two different carbonyl compounds; if both have α-H, four products form. Useful when one partner has **no α-H** (HCHO, C₆H₅CHO). **Cannizzaro:** aldehydes with **no α-H** + **concentrated** NaOH → alcohol + carboxylate salt (disproportionation, via hydride transfer). **Crossed Cannizzaro** with HCHO: HCHO is oxidised to methanoate, the other aldehyde reduced.

visual.alt: Table of aldol and Cannizzaro conditions

slides.narration: When two different carbonyl compounds both have alpha hydrogens, a cross aldol gives a mixture of four products, so it is most useful when one partner, such as methanal, has none. An aldehyde with no alpha hydrogen cannot form an enolate; with concentrated alkali, one molecule transfers a hydride to another, giving an alcohol and a carboxylate salt: the Cannizzaro reaction. With methanal present, methanal is always the one oxidised.

slides.heading: Worked example: aldol or Cannizzaro?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the products: (a) propanal + dilute NaOH, then heat; (b) 2,2-dimethylpropanal + conc. NaOH; (c) methanal + ethanal (dilute NaOH); (d) 4-methylbenzaldehyde + methanal + conc. NaOH.

**(a)** Aldol: 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal → 2-methylpent-2-enal.

**(b)** No α-H: Cannizzaro → 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol + sodium 2,2-dimethylpropanoate.

**(c)** Cross aldol: 3-hydroxypropanal.

**(d)** Crossed Cannizzaro: (4-methylphenyl)methanol + sodium methanoate.

visual.alt: Table classifying four cases

slides.narration: Look for alpha hydrogens and check the alkali concentration. Propanal has them, so dilute alkali gives the aldol, which dehydrates on heating. Two-two-dimethylpropanal has a quaternary carbon next to the aldehyde group and no alpha hydrogens, so it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction. Methanal and ethanal give a cross aldol. With methanal and an aromatic aldehyde in concentrated alkali, methanal is oxidised and the aromatic aldehyde reduced.

slides.heading: Quick check: aldol or Cannizzaro
slides.body_md: Decide which base-catalysed reaction occurs.
slides.narration: Quick check. Alpha hydrogens and dilute alkali: aldol. No alpha hydrogens and concentrated alkali: Cannizzaro.

slides.heading: Tests and uses
slides.body_md: **Aldehyde vs ketone:** Tollens’ reagent → silver mirror (aldehydes); Fehling’s / Benedict’s → red-brown Cu₂O (aliphatic aldehydes); Schiff’s reagent → pink (aldehydes). **Methanal vs ethanal:** iodoform (ethanal only). **Methyl ketone vs other ketone:** iodoform. **Uses:** methanal (formalin, Bakelite, urotropine), ethanal (ethanoic acid, ethyl ethanoate), propanone (solvent, nail-polish remover), butanone (solvent).

visual.alt: Table of tests for methanal, ethanal and propanone

slides.narration: Tollens’ reagent, ammoniacal silver nitrate, is reduced by aldehydes to a silver mirror; Fehling’s solution gives a red-brown precipitate of copper one oxide with aliphatic aldehydes. Ketones give neither. Methanal and ethanal both reduce these reagents, but only ethanal gives iodoform. Methanal is used as formalin and to make resins and urotropine; propanone is a common solvent.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Nucleophilic addition: HCHO > RCHO > R₂CO (+I, steric). HCN via CN⁻ (base catalyst) → cyanohydrin.
NaHSO₃ adducts; Grignard → alcohols; Z–NH₂ → oxime, hydrazone, phenylhydrazone, semicarbazone.
Aldehydes oxidised easily; iodoform for CH₃CO–; reduction to alcohols (NaBH₄) or alkanes (Clemmensen, Wolff–Kishner, red P/HI).
α-H acidic (enolate); aldol (dilute alkali) → β-hydroxy carbonyl → enal; cross aldol.
No α-H + conc. alkali: Cannizzaro; crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO.
Tests: Tollens’, Fehling’s, iodoform; uses of methanal, ethanal, propanone.

visual.alt: Summary table of key reactions

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Nucleophiles add to the carbonyl group, aldehydes more readily than ketones. Aldehydes are easily oxidised, which gives the Tollens’ and Fehling’s tests, while methyl ketones give iodoform. Carbonyl groups are reduced to alcohols or right down to CH two groups. Alpha hydrogens make the aldol reaction possible, and aldehydes without them undergo the Cannizzaro reaction.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Show CN⁻ formation and both steps in the HCN mechanism.
State dilute or concentrated alkali when predicting aldol or Cannizzaro.
For reduction to alkane, name the method and its condition (acid or base).
For tests, give observations for both compounds.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. In the hydrogen cyanide mechanism, show how cyanide ions are formed and both steps. Say whether the alkali is dilute or concentrated before choosing between aldol and Cannizzaro. Name the reduction method with its conditions. And in distinguishing tests, describe what happens with each compound.

sections.heading: 1. Nomenclature, structure and physical properties
sections.body_md:
Aldehydes **-al** (CHO = C-1): 3-methylbutanal; ketones **-one**: pentan-3-one, 3-methylbutan-2-one; dialdehydes **-dial**. Carbonyl C is **sp²**, planar, ≈ 120°; C=O polar (C δ+).

sections.heading: 2. Preparation
sections.body_md:
- **Alcohols:** 1° → RCHO (PCC; Cu, 573 K); 2° → ketone.
- **Alkenes:** ozonolysis (O₃; Zn/H₂O). **Alkynes:** H₂O/HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ — ethyne → ethanal; others → ketones.
- **Acid chlorides:** Rosenmund (H₂, Pd/BaSO₄) → RCHO; $\ce{2CH3COCl + (CH3)2Cd -> 2CH3COCH3 + CdCl2}$ → ketones.
- **Calcium salts:** $\ce{(CH3COO)2Ca -> CH3COCH3 + CaCO3}$; with calcium methanoate → aldehyde.
- **Nitriles:** Stephen (SnCl₂/HCl; H₂O) → RCHO; R′MgX then H₃O⁺ → ketone; DIBAL-H → RCHO. **Esters:** DIBAL-H → RCHO.

sections.heading: 4. Oxidation, iodoform and reduction
sections.body_md:
Aldehydes oxidised easily (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, Tollens’, Fehling’s); ketones only by strong oxidants with C–C cleavage. **Iodoform:** CH₃CO– (or CH₃CH(OH)–) + I₂/NaOH → yellow CHI₃ + carboxylate (one C fewer).

**Reduction:** NaBH₄/LiAlH₄/H₂–Ni → alcohols (1° from aldehydes, 2° from ketones). C=O → CH₂: **Clemmensen** (Zn–Hg, conc. HCl; acid); **Wolff–Kishner** (NH₂NH₂, then KOH/ethylene glycol, heat; base); **red P + HI**.

key_terms.definition_md: Reduction of C=O to CH₂ with zinc amalgam and conc. HCl.
Reduction of C=O to CH₂ via the hydrazone with KOH in ethylene glycol.

sections.heading: 5. Aldol, cross aldol and Cannizzaro
sections.body_md:
**α-H** acidic (enolate resonance). **Aldol** (dilute OH⁻): enolate attacks C=O of another molecule → β-hydroxy carbonyl → (heat) α,β-unsaturated carbonyl. $\ce{2CH3CHO -> CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO}$ → but-2-enal. **Cross aldol:** best with one partner lacking α-H (HCHO + CH₃CHO → 3-hydroxypropanal).

**Cannizzaro** (no α-H, conc. OH⁻): $\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$; crossed with HCHO: HCHO oxidised, the other aldehyde reduced.

key_terms.definition_md: A β-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone formed by base-catalysed self-addition of a carbonyl compound with α-H.
Disproportionation of an aldehyde without α-H in concentrated alkali to an alcohol and a carboxylate.

sections.heading: 6. Tests and uses
sections.body_md:
**Aldehyde vs ketone:** Tollens’ (silver mirror), Fehling’s (red-brown Cu₂O, aliphatic aldehydes), Schiff’s reagent (pink). **Methanal vs ethanal:** iodoform (ethanal +). **Methyl ketones:** iodoform. **2,4-DNP:** orange ppt for any C=O.

**Uses:** methanal — formalin, Bakelite and urea–formaldehyde resins, urotropine ((CH₂)₆N₄); ethanal — ethanoic acid, ethyl ethanoate; propanone — solvent, nail-polish remover; butanone — solvent.

key_terms.definition_md: Ammoniacal silver nitrate; reduced by aldehydes to a silver mirror.
Alkaline copper(II) tartrate; reduced by aliphatic aldehydes to red-brown Cu₂O.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Propyne hydration giving propanal (it gives propanone).
- Aldol with benzaldehyde or methanal alone (no α-H: Cannizzaro).
- Methanal giving iodoform (it does not).
- Confusing Clemmensen (acid) and Wolff–Kishner (base).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Mechanisms (2–3 marks): nucleophile formation, attack, protonation.
- Named preparations (1 mark each): reagent, condition and product.
- Tests (1–2 marks): reagent and observations for both compounds.

cards.front_md: Why do carbonyl compounds boil below alcohols?
Role of base in HCN addition?

cards.back_md: Check α-H and alkali strength first.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of isovaleraldehyde, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CHO, is:
questions.solution_md: The CHO carbon is C-1; methyl on C-3 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Diethyl ketone, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, has the IUPAC name:
questions.solution_md: Five-carbon chain, C=O at C-3 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In propanal, the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon and the approximate bond angle around it are:
Propanone (b.p. 329 K) boils higher than butane (b.p. 273 K) but lower than propan-1-ol (b.p. 370 K). The best explanation is that propanone molecules:

options.text_md: attract each other by dipole–dipole forces but cannot hydrogen-bond with one another
have a much larger molar mass than propan-1-ol

questions.solution_md: Polar C=O, but no O–H — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Lower aldehydes and ketones dissolve in water because water molecules form hydrogen bonds with the carbonyl oxygen.
questions.solution_md: True. The carbonyl oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water.

questions.stem_md: The IUPAC name of OHC–CH₂–CH₂–CHO is butane___.
Match each carbonyl compound with its IUPAC name.
questions.solution_md: Propionaldehyde = propanal; ethyl methyl ketone = butan-2-one; crotonaldehyde = but-2-enal; isobutyraldehyde = 2-methylpropanal.

questions.stem_md: Give the IUPAC names of (a) CH₃COCH(CH₃)₂ and (b) CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CHO.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) 3-Methylbutan-2-one. (b) 3-Methylpentanal.

questions.stem_md: Arrange butane, propanal and propan-1-ol (similar molar masses) in order of increasing boiling point, and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Butane < propanal < propan-1-ol. Butane has only weak dispersion forces; propanal has a polar C=O group and dipole–dipole attractions; propan-1-ol forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which are strongest.

questions.stem_md: Propanoyl chloride is reduced with hydrogen over palladium poisoned with barium sulphate. The product is:
questions.solution_md: Rosenmund reduction stops at the aldehyde — option (d).

questions.stem_md: 2-Methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, is treated with ozone and then zinc and water. The products are:
questions.solution_md: Cleaving the C=C gives (CH₃)₂C=O and O=CHCH₃ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with dimethylcadmium. The product is:
A mixture of calcium ethanoate and calcium methanoate is heated strongly. The main carbonyl product is:
Benzonitrile, C₆H₅CN, is treated with methylmagnesium iodide and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The compound formed is:
questions.solution_md: RCN + R′MgX → imine salt → ketone — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Ethyl ethanoate is treated with diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H) at low temperature and then water. The carbonyl product is:
questions.solution_md: DIBAL-H reduces esters to aldehydes — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the Rosenmund reduction the palladium catalyst is poisoned with barium sulphate.

**Reason (R):** A poisoned catalyst stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage, so the aldehyde is not reduced to an alcohol.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hydration of propyne with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄ gives propanal.
questions.solution_md: False. Markovnikov hydration gives propanone; only ethyne gives an aldehyde.

questions.stem_md: $15.8\ \text{g}$ of calcium ethanoate ($M = 158$) is heated: $\ce{(CH3COO)2Ca -> CH3COCH3 + CaCO3}$. What mass of propanone ($M = 58$) can be obtained at most?
Write equations for preparing (a) ethanal from ethyne and (b) butanone from ethanoyl chloride using a dialkylcadmium.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{HC#CH + H2O ->[HgSO4][dil. H2SO4] CH3CHO}$. (b) $\ce{2CH3COCl + (CH3CH2)2Cd -> 2CH3COCH2CH3 + CdCl2}$.

questions.stem_md: Describe the Stephen reaction, using propanenitrile as the example and naming the product.

answer.model_answer_md: Propanenitrile is reduced with tin(II) chloride and hydrochloric acid to the imine (as its hydrochloride), CH₃CH₂CH=NH·HCl; hydrolysis with water then gives propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, and ammonium chloride.

questions.stem_md: Suggest a reagent or method for each conversion and name the product: (a) butan-2-ol → a ketone; (b) calcium propanoate → a ketone; (c) ethanenitrile → a ketone using a Grignard reagent.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (or Cu at 573 K): butanone. (b) Heat (dry distillation): pentan-3-one, (CH₃CH₂COO)₂Ca → CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ + CaCO₃. (c) CH₃CH₂MgBr, then H₃O⁺: butanone (or C₆H₅MgBr → acetophenone).

questions.stem_md: An alkene C₅H₁₀ on ozonolysis gives propanone and ethanal. (a) Identify the alkene. (b) Name the two products by IUPAC rules. (c) What would but-1-ene give on ozonolysis?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) 2-Methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃. (b) Propanone (propan-2-one) and ethanal. (c) Propanal and methanal.

questions.stem_md: Arrange methanal, ethanal and butanone in order of decreasing reactivity towards hydrogen cyanide.

options.text_md: all react at the same rate

questions.solution_md: More alkyl groups: less δ+ on carbon and more steric hindrance — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A trace of base speeds up the addition of HCN to propanone because:

options.text_md: it converts HCN into CN⁻, the actual nucleophile
it removes the cyanohydrin as it forms

questions.solution_md: HCN + OH⁻ → CN⁻ + H₂O; CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Ethanal is shaken with saturated sodium hydrogensulphite solution. A crystalline solid separates. This reaction is used to:

options.text_md: separate and purify aldehydes from mixtures

questions.solution_md: The bisulphite adduct is filtered and decomposed by acid or alkali to recover the aldehyde — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Propanal reacts with hydroxylamine, NH₂OH. The product is:
questions.solution_md: Addition then loss of water gives C=N–OH — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Ethylmagnesium bromide is added to ethanal and the product is hydrolysed. The alcohol obtained is:
questions.solution_md: RMgX + R′CHO → secondary alcohol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Propanone is less reactive than propanal towards nucleophilic addition.

**Reason (R):** Propanone has two electron-releasing methyl groups, whereas propanal has a carbonyl hydrogen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the two alkyl groups reduce δ+ on carbon and hinder attack — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hydrolysis of ethanal cyanohydrin gives 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid).
The derivative formed when propanone reacts with semicarbazide, NH₂NHCONH₂, is called propanone ___.
Explain why aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition, using ethanal and propanone as examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Electronic: propanone has two methyl groups (+I) that reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon; ethanal has only one. Steric: two alkyl groups crowd the carbonyl carbon in propanone more than one methyl and a hydrogen in ethanal, hindering the approach of the nucleophile.

questions.stem_md: Write the products of ethanal with (a) phenylhydrazine and (b) 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, and state why such derivatives are useful.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Ethanal phenylhydrazone, CH₃CH=NNHC₆H₅ (+ H₂O). (b) Ethanal 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, an orange/yellow solid (+ H₂O). These are crystalline solids with sharp, characteristic melting points, used to identify the parent carbonyl compound; the 2,4-DNP precipitate also tests for C=O.

questions.stem_md: Give the mechanism of the base-catalysed addition of hydrogen cyanide to propanal.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) $\ce{HCN + OH- -> CN- + H2O}$ (CN⁻ generated). (2) CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon of propanal (slow), the π electrons move to oxygen, giving the tetrahedral alkoxide $\ce{CH3CH2CH(O-)CN}$. (3) The alkoxide takes H⁺ from HCN (or water), giving the cyanohydrin $\ce{CH3CH2CH(OH)CN}$ and regenerating CN⁻.

questions.stem_md: Give the product of propanone with (a) sodium hydrogensulphite, (b) hydrazine and (c) phenylmagnesium bromide followed by hydrolysis.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) (CH₃)₂C(OH)SO₃Na, the bisulphite adduct. (b) (CH₃)₂C=NNH₂, propanone hydrazone (+ H₂O). (c) 2-Phenylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)C₆H₅.

questions.stem_md: Butanone is heated with hydrazine and then with KOH in ethylene glycol. The organic product is:
Which of these gives a yellow precipitate with iodine and NaOH: pentan-3-one, pentan-2-one, propanal or methanal?
questions.solution_md: Only pentan-2-one has a CH₃CO– group — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The Clemmensen reduction is unsuitable for a carbonyl compound that also contains an acid-sensitive group because it uses:

options.text_md: zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid

questions.solution_md: Clemmensen is strongly acidic; Wolff–Kishner (basic) is used instead — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Pentan-3-one is reduced with sodium borohydride. The product is:

**Assertion (A):** Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens’ reagent but ketones are not.

**Reason (R):** Ketones contain no carbonyl group.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true (aldehydes have an oxidisable C–H on the carbonyl carbon). R is false — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Heating propanone with hydrogen iodide and red phosphorus gives propane.
$1.44\ \text{g}$ of butanone ($M = 72$) reacts completely with iodine and NaOH: $\ce{CH3COCH2CH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 + CH3CH2COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O}$. What mass of iodoform ($M = 394$) forms?
Compare the Clemmensen and Wolff–Kishner reductions: give the reagents for each and the product from propanone.

answer.model_answer_md: Clemmensen: zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl (acidic). Wolff–Kishner: hydrazine, then KOH (or C₂H₅ONa) in ethylene glycol on heating (basic). Both convert propanone to propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃.

questions.stem_md: Name the product when butanal is treated with (a) LiAlH₄, (b) Zn–Hg and conc. HCl and (c) Tollens’ reagent.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Butan-1-ol. (b) Butane (Clemmensen). (c) Butanoate ion (butanoic acid on acidification), with a silver mirror.

questions.stem_md: 2,2-Dimethylpropanal, (CH₃)₃CCHO, is warmed with concentrated NaOH. It undergoes:

options.text_md: the Cannizzaro reaction, because it has no α-hydrogen

questions.solution_md: No α-H, concentrated alkali → disproportionation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The α-hydrogens of propanal are acidic because:

options.text_md: the C–H bond is very long
they are bonded to the carbonyl oxygen
the enolate ion formed is stabilised by resonance with the carbonyl oxygen

questions.solution_md: Negative charge delocalised onto O — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Methanal and ethanal are treated together with dilute NaOH. The main cross-aldol product is:
questions.solution_md: Ethanal enolate attacks methanal (no α-H) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Butanal undergoes aldol condensation with dilute NaOH, and the aldol is heated. The final product is:

**Assertion (A):** Benzaldehyde undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated NaOH.

**Reason (R):** Benzaldehyde has two α-hydrogens.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, which is why it gives Cannizzaro — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In aldol condensation the enolate ion acts as a nucleophile.

**Reason (R):** The enolate ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second carbonyl molecule.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the crossed Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde with methanal, benzaldehyde is oxidised and methanal is reduced.
questions.solution_md: False. Methanal is oxidised to methanoate; benzaldehyde is reduced to phenylmethanol.

questions.stem_md: $0.20\ \text{mol}$ of methanal undergoes complete Cannizzaro reaction with concentrated NaOH: $\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$. What mass of methanol ($M = 32$) forms?
Write the aldol and the dehydration product formed from propanal with dilute NaOH.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{2CH3CH2CHO ->[dil. NaOH] CH3CH2CH(OH)CH(CH3)CHO}$ (3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal); on heating it loses water: $\ce{CH3CH2CH=C(CH3)CHO}$, 2-methylpent-2-enal.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for the crossed Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde with methanal in concentrated NaOH, and explain which aldehyde is oxidised.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{C6H5CHO + HCHO + NaOH -> C6H5CH2OH + HCOONa}$. Methanal is oxidised (to methanoate) because its carbonyl carbon is the most reactive towards OH⁻, so it forms the intermediate that transfers hydride; benzaldehyde accepts the hydride and is reduced.

questions.stem_md: Give the mechanism of the aldol reaction of ethanal with dilute NaOH.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) $\ce{OH-}$ removes an α-H: $\ce{CH3CHO + OH- -> CH2CHO- + H2O}$; the enolate is resonance-stabilised. (2) The enolate carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second ethanal molecule, giving the alkoxide $\ce{CH3CH(O-)CH2CHO}$. (3) The alkoxide takes H⁺ from water: $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO}$ (3-hydroxybutanal) and OH⁻ is regenerated.

questions.stem_md: State, with reasons, whether each compound undergoes aldol condensation or the Cannizzaro reaction with alkali: (a) propanone, (b) methanal, (c) 2-methylpropanal.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Aldol (dilute alkali): it has α-hydrogens (six). (b) Cannizzaro (concentrated alkali): no α-hydrogen. (c) Aldol: it has one α-hydrogen on C-2.

questions.stem_md: Which of these does NOT reduce Fehling’s solution: methanal, ethanal, propanal or propanone?
questions.solution_md: Ketones are not oxidised by Fehling’s solution — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which test distinguishes ethanal from methanal?

options.text_md: Iodoform test (warm with I₂ and NaOH)

questions.solution_md: Only ethanal has CH₃CO–; both reduce Tollens’ and Fehling’s, both give 2,4-DNP — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Methanal reacts with ammonia to give urotropine (hexamine), used as a urinary antiseptic. Its formula is:
A 40% aqueous solution of methanal, used to preserve biological specimens, is called ___.
$0.58\ \text{g}$ of propanal ($M = 58$) is oxidised completely by Fehling’s solution: $\ce{RCHO + 2Cu^2+ + 5OH- -> RCOO- + Cu2O + 3H2O}$. What mass of copper(I) oxide ($M = 143$) precipitates?
Give one chemical test, with observations, to distinguish (a) propanal from propanone and (b) pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Tollens’ reagent: propanal gives a silver mirror; propanone does not (or Fehling’s: red-brown precipitate with propanal only). (b) Iodoform test (I₂/NaOH, warm): pentan-2-one gives a yellow precipitate of CHI₃; pentan-3-one does not.

questions.stem_md: A compound X, C₄H₈O, gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNP and a yellow precipitate with iodine and NaOH, but does not reduce Tollens’ reagent. (a) Identify X. (b) Write the equation for its iodoform reaction. (c) What would X give with NaBH₄?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) X is a methyl ketone (C=O present; not an aldehyde; CH₃CO–): butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃. (b) $\ce{CH3COCH2CH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 + CH3CH2COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O}$. (c) Butan-2-ol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations for preparing (i) propanal by the Rosenmund reduction and (ii) propanone from calcium ethanoate. [2]

(b) How is butanone obtained from ethanenitrile using a Grignard reagent? [1½]

(c) Explain why propanone boils higher than butane but lower than propan-1-ol. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) $\ce{CH3CH2COCl + H2 ->[Pd/BaSO4] CH3CH2CHO + HCl}$. (ii) $\ce{(CH3COO)2Ca ->[\Delta] CH3COCH3 + CaCO3}$.

(b) Ethylmagnesium bromide adds to the nitrile carbon to give an imine salt, CH₃C(=NMgBr)CH₂CH₃, which dilute acid hydrolyses to butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃.

(c) Propanone is polar (dipole–dipole forces), so it boils above non-polar butane, but it has no O–H and cannot hydrogen-bond with itself, unlike propan-1-ol.

questions.solution_md: Rosenmund; calcium salt; Grignard + nitrile; b.p.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give the mechanism of the addition of HCN to ethanal, including the role of the base. [2]

(b) Why is methanal more reactive than propanone towards nucleophiles? [1]

(c) Give the products of propanone with (i) NaHSO₃, (ii) hydroxylamine and (iii) CH₃MgI followed by hydrolysis. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{HCN + OH- -> CN- + H2O}$; CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon (slow) giving $\ce{CH3CH(O-)CN}$; protonation by HCN gives the cyanohydrin $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CN}$ and regenerates CN⁻. The base generates the nucleophile.

(b) Methanal has no alkyl groups: its carbonyl carbon is more positive and less hindered.

(c) (i) $\ce{(CH3)2C(OH)SO3Na}$. (ii) Propanone oxime, $\ce{(CH3)2C=NOH}$. (iii) 2-Methylpropan-2-ol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are α-hydrogens, and why are they acidic? [1]

(b) Give the mechanism of the aldol condensation of ethanal and name the product formed on heating. [2½]

(c) Write the equation for the Cannizzaro reaction of methanal and explain why ethanal does not undergo this reaction. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Hydrogens on the carbon next to C=O; removing one gives an enolate stabilised by resonance (charge on O).

(b) $\ce{OH-}$ removes an α-H to give the enolate $\ce{CH2CHO-}$; this attacks the C=O of another ethanal; the alkoxide is protonated by water to give 3-hydroxybutanal (aldol). On heating it loses water to give but-2-enal, $\ce{CH3CH=CHCHO}$.

(c) $\ce{2HCHO + NaOH -> HCOONa + CH3OH}$. Ethanal has α-hydrogens, so with alkali it forms an enolate and undergoes aldol condensation instead.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations for the oxidation of ethanal by Tollens’ reagent and by Fehling’s solution, and state the observations. [2]

(b) Give the reagents and conditions for reducing butanone to (i) butan-2-ol and (ii) butane by two different methods. [2]

(c) Which of propanal, butanone and pentan-3-one give the iodoform test? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{CH3CHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH- -> CH3COO- + 2Ag + 2H2O + 4NH3}$: silver mirror. $\ce{CH3CHO + 2Cu^2+ + 5OH- -> CH3COO- + Cu2O + 3H2O}$: red-brown precipitate.

(b) (i) NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄, or H₂/Ni). (ii) Clemmensen: Zn–Hg, conc. HCl; Wolff–Kishner: NH₂NH₂, then KOH in ethylene glycol, heat (or red P + HI).

(c) Only butanone (CH₃CO–).

questions.stem_md:
Three compounds A, B and C have the formula C₃H₆O. A gives a silver mirror with Tollens’ reagent; B gives a yellow precipitate with I₂/NaOH but no silver mirror; C decolourises bromine water and reacts with sodium, liberating hydrogen.

(a) Identify A, B and C. [3]

(b) Write the equation for the reaction of B with HCN. [1]

(c) What does A give with dilute NaOH? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A: propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO (aldehyde). B: propanone, CH₃COCH₃ (methyl ketone). C: prop-2-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH (C=C and –OH).

(b) CH₃COCH₃ + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.

(c) Aldol condensation: 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal (and 2-methylpent-2-enal on heating).
